memoryText: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Numbers 6:24-26 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
The Aaronic blessing is one of the oldest pieces of Scripture still used in worship. It has been said over God’s people for three thousand years. Receive it as if it is spoken to you today.

“The LORD bless you and keep you.” The blessing begins with God’s goodness and protection. To keep means to guard and watch over, as a shepherd keeps his flock. It does not promise a life without trouble. It promises the one who keeps us in trouble.

“The LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you.” The face of God shining is a picture of his favor and delight. A father’s smile gives a child confidence. God’s face, turned toward you in grace, is the deepest blessing there is.

“The LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.” The picture is of God looking at you, lifting his face, and giving shalom. Peace here is not only calm. It means wholeness, the well-being of every part of life.

Notice that the name of the LORD stands at the start of each line. He is the one who blesses, and he does it by putting his name on his people. For Christians, this is fulfilled in Christ. In him, God’s face has shone on us (2 Corinthians 4:6), and he has made peace through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20).
weekInReview: This week you began the book of Numbers. You read about the census of Israel and the arrangement of the camp around the tabernacle, and you saw that God knows his people by name. You read about the Levites, who were given to God in place of the firstborn, and who carried the tabernacle with reverence. You read laws of purity and restitution, the Nazirite vow, and the blessing that God commanded Aaron to speak over his people. In Psalm 90, you heard Moses pray about the brevity of life and the eternity of God. The week taught that God orders and protects his people, that he claims them by substitution, and that he blesses them with his own name.
reflectionQuestions: The camp was arranged around the tabernacle. What is at the center of your life, and how would your daily schedule change if God’s presence were at the center?
The Levites were taken in place of the firstborn. How does the idea of substitution deepen your understanding of what Christ did for you?
Psalm 90 asks, “Teach us to number our days.” What is one thing you would do differently if you took the shortness of life seriously?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for blessing and keeping you this week, naming one way.
Thank him for putting his name on his people.
